exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with suspected hypertension and why? — BP measurement on two occasions confirms diagnosis and guides treatment
A patient with type 2 diabetes presents with sudden leg swelling. What is the most likely complication and what test confirms it? — Acute kidney injury; serum creatinine rise
During a ward round you find a patient with chronic cough and sputum. What bedside test can you perform to rule out COPD? — Peak expiratory flow or spirometry if available
A 55‑year‑old man with known hypertension develops chest pain. What is the next step and why? — ECG to rule out acute coronary syndrome
You suspect CKD in a patient with HIV. Which drug class should you avoid and why? — NSAIDs, they worsen renal perfusion
A patient on metformin develops nausea and abdominal pain. What is the emergency concern and immediate action? — Lactic acidosis; stop metformin and give IV fluids
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Non‑communicable diseases (NCDs) are chronic conditions that dominate morbidity in East Africa. Clinicians must recognise patterns, use limited tests, and prioritise cost‑effective management.

b: Hypertension: BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions
Diabetes: Fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL or random ≥200 mg/dL
COPD: Persistent dyspnoea, cough, spirometry FEV1/FVC <0.7
sections.p: NCDs are chronic, non‑infectious conditions such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease and COPD. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, basic investigations and simple screening tools.

b: Hypertension: Stage 1 140–159/90–99, Stage 2 ≥160/100
Diabetes: HbA1c <7% good control, >8% poor
CKD: Stage 1–5 by eGFR, Stage 5 requires dialysis
COPD: GOLD A–D based on symptoms and exacerbation risk
sections.p: Staging uses WHO or national guidelines to guide treatment intensity and monitoring.

b: Behavioural: tobacco, alcohol, sedentary lifestyle
Metabolic: obesity, dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance
Infectious: HIV, TB, hepatitis B, malaria can precipitate CKD
Environmental: biomass smoke, air pollution
Genetic: family history, sickle cell, thalassaemia
sections.p: Risk factors cluster with infectious diseases and traditional practices.

b: Hypertension: headache, visual blurring, chest pain
Diabetes: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss
CKD: oedema, fatigue, anaemia
COPD: chronic cough, sputum, exertional dyspnoea
sections.p: Symptoms are often vague; look for red flags that suggest organ involvement or complications.
Use tests that are affordable and available; interpret with clinical context.

t.b: Assess hypertension severity; a reading ≥140/90 mmHg on two visits confirms hypertension
Screen for diabetes; a value ≥200 mg/dL suggests diabetes
Estimate kidney function; eGFR <60 indicates CKD
Rule out pneumonia, heart failure; look for hyperinflation in COPD
Detect ischemic changes in suspected heart disease

b: Hypertension: chest pain, haemoptysis, visual loss
Diabetes: ketoacidosis symptoms, severe hypoglycaemia
CKD: sudden rise in creatinine, pulmonary oedema
COPD: acute exacerbation with increased sputum colour, cyanosis
sections.p: Urgent signs require immediate referral or intervention.

b: Hypertension: lifestyle (salt reduction, exercise), ACE inhibitors or ARBs, avoid NSAIDs
Diabetes: diet, metformin (if no renal impairment), insulin for ketoacidosis
CKD: ACE/ARB, salt restriction, avoid nephrotoxins, plan dialysis
COPD: bronchodilators (SABA, LABA), inhaled steroids if frequent exacerbations, avoid smoking
sections.p: Treat underlying cause, provide supportive care and monitor with simple tools.

b: BP and glucose checks every 3–6 months
Annual urine albumin test for diabetics
Smoking cessation programmes
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus
sections.p: Regular monitoring, community education and early screening are key.

b: HbA1c may be falsely low in haemolytic anaemia
eGFR overestimates function in low muscle mass
Spirometry requires patient effort; poor technique gives false normal
sections.p: Low sensitivity of tests in low‑resource settings can mask disease.
